The study uses a 2-layer Dällenbach type radar absorber design with composite laminates as lossy layers.
Carbon nanotubes (CNT) were added to epoxy resin at weight percentages of 1.5, 2.0, 3.0, 3.5, and 4.0 wt% to control electromagnetic properties.
E-glass fabric used is plain weave with fiber counts of 60 and 57 yarns/in warp and fill directions, respectively, and fiber aerial weight of 107 g/m2.
Composite laminates were cured in an autoclave at 80 ºC for 30 minutes and 120 ºC for over 2 hours.
Nominal ply thickness is about 0.111 ± 0.02 mm, increasing slightly with CNT content.
Complex permittivity was measured from 0.5 to 18 GHz using a vector network analyzer and coaxial airline.
The characteristic impedance and propagation constant in the absorber layers depend on complex permittivity; permeability is assumed unity.
Optimization targeted reflection loss at 10 GHz, the center frequency of the X-band (8.2–12.4 GHz).
Genetic algorithm was used to optimize ply numbers and CNT content for minimal reflection loss.
The optimized design for CASE 1 had 32 plies of pure E-glass/epoxy and 11 plies of CNT composite with 5.27 wt% CNT.
Measured laminate thicknesses were 2.88 mm for the first layer and 1.40 mm for the second layer, close to design values.
The fabricated absorber achieved a -10 dB reflection loss bandwidth of 7.4 GHz.
Discrepancies between design and measurement were attributed to discrete ply thickness and permittivity differences.
The reflection loss curve shows two peaks; the spacing between these peaks affects broadband absorption performance.
CNTs are mainly distributed in the resin-rich areas between E-glass fibers, enhancing electrical conductivity.
The epoxy resin was diluted with acetone to lower viscosity and allow higher CNT loading before evaporation.
The complex permittivity model includes frequency-dependent dielectric constant and conductivity terms fitted semi-empirically.
The input impedance of each layer is calculated recursively using transmission line theory.
The reflection coefficient formula incorporates characteristic impedance and propagation constant of each layer.
The study confirms that controlling electromagnetic properties and layer thickness is critical for broadband radar absorption.
